answer: Use show spectrum-monitoring-<name>/<direction>/<center-frequency> [width] [lower-frequency] [upper-frequency] [target-actual-power] [power-actual] [psd-actual]. name is a string 0..64; direction is ingress or egress, default egress, and only egress is currently supported; center-frequency is the band slice center frequency in MHz and is managed by the system. width is the received NMC width in MHz, default 50000. lower-frequency and upper-frequency give the media channel edges in MHz. power-actual is the currently received power in dBm, default -99; -99 dBm means the power has not yet been measured by the OCM on the DGE2 card, or no power was detected (or no appropriate fiber connection). For egress, power-actual is calibrated at the DWDM line port output, the same reference point where target power is defined. target-actual-power is the ATPS-calculated target, default -99 dBm, relevant only when target-power-setting = auto. psd-actual is the calculated Power Spectral Density in nW/GHz to 2 digit precision, default not-applicable, and does not depend on spectra width. Example: show spectrum-monitoring-1-7-dwdm-line2/egress/191968750. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Read the contention-check-status attribute on the super channel. You can pass it on add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value> [label] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [contention-check-status], and read it with show super-channel-<name> ... [contention-check-status]. It is the Contention Check state set via DNA in openwave mode, with values pending, success, overridden and failk, defaulting to pending. It is only applicable if openwave-contention-check is enabled at the super-channel-group level; that attribute enables the DNA assisted contention control mechanism in openwave mode, takes false or true, and defaults to false. So enable openwave-contention-check on the super-channel-group first, otherwise contention-check-status stays meaningless. Related power context on the super channel: line-system-mode defaults to openwave, and expected-total-tx-power (theoretical total TX power at the faceplate, computed from per-carrier target TX power) defaults to -55.

-m is the merge configuration flag. The add command for super-channel-group works in merge mode only, so -m performs a best effort add: if the target entity does not exist it is created, and if it already exists it is updated with whatever attributes are present on the add command. In other words the command will not fail if the entity already exists. Full syntax: add -m super-channel-group-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <lock|unlock|maintenance>] [auto-in-service-enabled <value>] [valid-signal-time <value>] [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>] [line-system-mode <value>] [openwave-contention-check <value>]. Defaults on that object: admin-state unlock, alarm-report-control allowed, auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes (range 1..7200), line-system-mode openwave, managed-by user, oper-state disabled. The same -m merge behaviour applies to comm-channel.

Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], which displays the list of supported carrier modes. carrier-mode is an acronymized code (handle) for the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, string length 1..15, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, so that attribute answers the capacity question per mode. client-mode is the digital client mode mapped into and transported by the carriers in the superchannel, either ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate. application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string length 1..15. compatibility-id identifies which carrier modes can be applied simultaneously. status is the state of the carrier mode. supported-subtypes lists subtypes each carrier mode supports, string 0..32 with a maximum of 20 elements. Access: Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max]. gain-range-type takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min is the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range (standard, low or high) and gain-range-max is the maximum settable gain-target for that range; both are of type gain-value with no default. So the numeric limits behind the low, standard and high settings are not fixed constants in the command definition, they are reported per entity by these two read-only attributes. The command is display only, available in Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

A card type can expose several power profiles because different profiles reflect different scenarios when using that card. The user defines, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. Inspect them with show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default]. card-type is the card type string and name is the profile name. profile-description is a string 0..255 describing the profile. power-draw is a decimal64 giving the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power. default is true or false, indicating whether that profile is the default value. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

It depends on router-id-mode. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and the same optional attributes are settable with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. router-id-mode takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, meaning by default the router ID is taken from the loopback IP. Set router-id-mode manual and supply router-id to specify it yourself. router-id accepts an IPv4 or IPv6 address, but 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. instance-id is a string 1..255, local-as is mandatory on add and ranges 1..4294967295, description is a string 0..128, and vrf is read only via show. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback.

Defaults on bgp-neighbor are connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535), hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535), and keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845). The guide notes hold-time is typically 3x the keepalive-interval and keepalive-interval is typically 1/3 the hold-time. negotiated-hold-time is a show-only value, 0..65535 seconds, default 0. Yes, you can authenticate the session: secure-session sets the authentication method to none or TCP-MD5, default none, and password carries the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII, string 0..80. Syntax: add bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> peer-as <value> [afi-safis] [enabled] [description] [secure-session] [password] [connect-retry-interval] [hold-time] [keepalive-interval]; all of those except peer-as and afi-safis are also changeable with set. enabled defaults to true; setting it false ceases an ESTABLISHED session and blocks both outgoing and incoming TCP attempts.

The route has to be in the forwarding table already. The guide states that routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. For routes not present in the IGP tables you must configure blackhole static routes: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole, for example on ipv4-static-route or ipv6-static-route where special-next-hop takes the value blackhole. Then create the bgp-network object with add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>; a maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured. instance-id is a string 1..255, remote-address is the peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported), and network-prefix is a decimal 1..64 or 128. Example: add bgp-network-10/2620:38:4001:192::65/3000::2/64.

mtu on comm-channel is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when mode is L3 (mode values are L1 ETH User Channel, L2 iGCC interface, L3 IP mode, default L3). It is a uint16 with a platform dependent range: 1280..1500 octets on 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500; for 1830 GX G40 the per interface type defaults are 1518 for DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Set it with add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [... mtu <value> ...] or set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>. Related L3-only attributes: mru 64..1500 octets default 1500, restart-timer 1..10 seconds default 3, max-failure 2..10 default 5, peer-address default 0.0.0.0. Example: add comm-channel-gcc0 type GCC0 label GCC0 alarm-report-control allowed mtu 1500 parent otu-1-6-1-OTUC4.

LLDP is off by default. lldp-admin-status defaults to disabled, meaning the agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames; the other values are tx-only, rx-only and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if mode is L1. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP is used as the management address and must be set explicitly by the user; it applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx, and takes 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only) or L0-MGMT. It is empty by default, in which case the system uses the loopback IP if configured, otherwise the DCN/AUX IP, and sends no TLV if neither has an address. Auto-negotiation is on: auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum) defaults to maximum, duplex-mode defaults to full, and flow-control defaults to disabled, but all three are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled. Example: set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx.

Use set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>] and read it back with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. mode takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6 and defaults to disabled, so relay is off until you change it. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. You can do both in one command, for example set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3, or just the mode with set dhcp-relay mode ipv4. This is the global setting; individual interfaces are enabled separately with set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, which obeys these global dhcp-relay settings. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts DNS servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and view with show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search]. enabled is a true/false flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, default true. search is the DNS search suffix name, string 0..64, and it must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Per-server origin is tracked separately on dns-server, where origin is dhcp or manual. Examples: set DNS enabled true and show DNS.

Add one with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. Remove with delete dns-server-<address>, change with set dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], and inspect with show dns-server-<address> [origin]. The origin attribute is how you tell where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address was manually configured. The default is manual. You can also use it in the other direction: the user can convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is per interface. Syntax: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>] and show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, string 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled takes true or false and defaults to false, so relay is off on an interface until you enable it. It enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface only and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global set dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (default disabled) with at least one server-address configured for it to do anything. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and read it back with show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

By default it is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [...], ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode takes unknown, protected or unprotected and defaults to protected (protected means backed by redundant ports, unprotected means no port redundancy); protection-state is the read-only current state and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock, oper-state disabled, alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (applicable only to the DCN interface), if-dhcp-relay false. if-type is show-only and takes ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc. Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is exactly what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings certain destinations and the result takes action on configured static routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into failed state and takes none or withdraw, defaulting to withdraw, so route withdrawal is the default behaviour. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6). next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the monitoring instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is the time between two consecutive pings, 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10 percent steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled defaults to true. The affected route reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. Read it with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Type ? after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask and only valid netmasks are allowed. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Certain addresses are disallowed: those beginning with 0 (current network), those beginning with 127 (loopback), and those beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). origin is show-only and takes static, dhcp or auto-config, default static, where static means configured through NETCONF or the CLI, dhcp means assigned by a DHCP server, and auto-config means created by autoconfiguration. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes exist because routes advertised to an external AS must be in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for routes not present in the IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Other attributes: advertised true/false, default false, which when set advertises the route in the routing protocol and, for OSPF, as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR; origin manual or dhcp, default manual; the interface VRF must match the static-route VRF. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

Nearly, but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask. Use add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed. Note that IPv6 /127 subnets are currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and do not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. origin is show-only and takes static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Use ? after ipv6-address- to list the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Pass interface DCN-B on the route. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Syntax: add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. The VRF bound to the interface must match the VRF given on the static route. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B, versus the primary case add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN. Defaults: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), special-next-hop blackhole, monitoring-state unmonitored. Access: Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each one must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to that LLDP neighbor. direction is ingress or egress. address is a string 0..64 identifying the management address component of the remote system, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface type associated with the address and takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. if-id is the integer interface number for that management address component on the remote system. address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity associated with the address advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in scope and key. management-address covers the addresses learned per direction, keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, so it includes a direction component of ingress or egress. management-address-local reports the management address information from the local LLDP ports and drops that component: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>. Both accept [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], both are read-only, and both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. if-subtype takes unknown (interface not known), if-index (identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object) or system-port-number (identifier based on the system port numbering convention). On management-address-local the address-oid field, a string 0..128, is currently an empty string. Example: show management-address-local.

Yes, it is the use-as-source attribute of the networking object. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it with show networking [use-as-source]. use-as-source names the interface to use as the source address and takes a string of length 0..64; no default is defined. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

show networking-services. It is used to show the list of network services and takes no command parameters, so there is nothing to qualify or filter. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This is distinct from the networking command (set networking / show networking), which handles the use-as-source attribute naming the interface to use as source address.
